title: From Military Radar to Modern Ergonomics: The Fascinating History of the Trackball
summary: Discover how a secret military invention turned into one of the most enduring alternative input devices for modern ergonomic workspaces.
whyBuy: Understanding the hardware history of the trackball illuminates why stationary pointing devices remain a premier choice for relieving wrist strain and optimizing compact desk setups today.
advantages: Originally invented in 1946 for Royal Canadian Navy radar plotting
Eliminates repetitive wrist sliding movements associated with traditional mice
Paved the way for modern optical tracking and ergonomic station design
body:
Long before optical sensors tracked our movements across sleek mousepads, the trackball was quietly shaping the future of human-computer interaction. Its origins date back to 1946, when naval officer Tom Cranston and his team developed a rudimentary system using a fivepin bowling ball and hardware rollers to track radar coordinates on a cathode-ray tube screen. This secret military project was called the Comprehensive Display System (CDS).

The Commercial Pivot

Despite its early military utility, the trackball didn't immediately find its way onto office desks. It wasn't until the 1960s that engineer Ken Kenyon and his colleagues at the Stanford Research Institute refined the mechanism for computer usage, eventually leading to commercial adaptations in CAD workstations, medical equipment, and arcade games like Missile Command.

Why Ergonomists Still Love It

In the modern workspace, the trackball has experienced a resurgence among developers, graphic designers, and office workers suffering from repetitive strain injuries (RSI). Unlike a standard mouse that requires sweeping arm and wrist motions, a trackball allows the hand to remain completely stationary while fingers or the thumb navigate the cursor. At Workspace Lab, we view the humble trackball not just as a retro novelty, but as a brilliant exercise in enduring ergonomic engineering.
